title: Solids — 20 MCQs
description: Covers energy levels and energy bands in solids, classification of metals, semiconductors and insulators on the basis of energy bands, intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, and the formation of p-type and n-type semiconductors.

questions.q: In an isolated atom the electrons occupy
questions.explanation: Isolated atoms have sharp, discrete energy levels for their electrons.

questions.q: When atoms come close to form a solid the discrete energy levels split into
questions.explanation: Interatomic interaction causes each atomic level to split into a large number of closely spaced levels that form energy bands.

questions.q: The energy gap between the valence band and the conduction band is called the
questions.explanation: The forbidden energy gap (band gap) is the energy range where no electron states exist.

questions.q: In a metal the valence band and conduction band
options: are separated by a large gap
questions.explanation: Metals have overlapping valence and conduction bands (or a partially filled conduction band), allowing free movement of electrons.

questions.q: An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure semiconductor in which
options: the number of free electrons equals the number of holes
questions.explanation: In an intrinsic semiconductor thermally generated electrons and holes are equal in number.

questions.q: A semiconductor has a forbidden energy gap of the order of
questions.explanation: Typical semiconductor band gaps are around 1 eV (e.g., Si ≈ 1.1 eV, Ge ≈ 0.7 eV).

questions.q: An insulator is characterized by a forbidden energy gap of approximately
questions.explanation: Insulators have large band gaps (typically > 3 eV), so electrons cannot easily jump to the conduction band at room temperature.

questions.q: n-type semiconductors are formed by doping a pure semiconductor with
questions.explanation: Pentavalent (donor) atoms such as P or As contribute extra electrons, making the semiconductor n-type.

questions.q: p-type semiconductors are formed by doping a pure semiconductor with
questions.explanation: Trivalent (acceptor) atoms such as B or Al create holes, making the semiconductor p-type.

questions.q: In an n-type semiconductor the majority charge carriers are
questions.explanation: Donor impurities provide free electrons that become the majority carriers in n-type material.

questions.q: In a p-type semiconductor the majority charge carriers are
questions.explanation: Acceptor impurities create holes that act as the majority carriers in p-type material.

questions.q: The Fermi level in an intrinsic semiconductor lies
options: approximately in the middle of the forbidden gap
questions.explanation: In pure semiconductors the Fermi level is located near the centre of the band gap.

questions.q: When a pentavalent atom is added to pure silicon, it acts as a
questions.explanation: The fifth valence electron of the pentavalent atom is loosely bound and can be donated to the conduction band.

questions.q: The resistivity of an intrinsic semiconductor
questions.explanation: Higher temperature generates more electron-hole pairs, increasing conductivity and therefore decreasing resistivity.

questions.q: Germanium is doped with arsenic. The resulting semiconductor is
questions.explanation: Arsenic is pentavalent and acts as a donor impurity, producing an n-type semiconductor.

questions.q: Silicon is doped with boron. The resulting semiconductor is
questions.explanation: Boron is trivalent and acts as an acceptor impurity, producing a p-type semiconductor.

questions.q: In an energy-band diagram the conduction band is the
options: lowest empty or partially filled band that allows conduction
questions.explanation: The conduction band is the lowest energy band that is empty or partially filled and in which electrons can move freely under an applied field.

questions.q: The energy gap of silicon is 1.1 eV. The minimum energy of a photon that can generate an electron-hole pair in silicon is
questions.explanation: A photon must supply at least the band-gap energy (1.1 eV) to excite an electron from the valence band to the conduction band.

questions.q: At absolute zero an intrinsic semiconductor behaves as
questions.explanation: At 0 K the valence band is completely filled and the conduction band is empty; no free carriers exist, so the material is insulating.

questions.q: The number of free electrons in an intrinsic semiconductor is equal to the number of holes. If the semiconductor is doped with a donor impurity the Fermi level
options: remains in the middle of the gap
questions.explanation: Donor doping increases the electron concentration, shifting the Fermi level upward toward the conduction band.
